h1: Calculate Your Dog's Daily Calorie Needs by Breed and Age
description: Calculate daily calories your dog needs by breed, weight, age and activity. Uses veterinary MER formula validated by WSAVA. Free and instant.
seoKeywords: how many calories does my dog need
intro:
The **daily calorie requirement** for a dog is determined using the veterinary formula known as **MER (Maintenance Energy Requirement)**, the same standard used by WSAVA (World Small Animal Veterinary Association), FEDIAF, and AAFCO. The core equation is **MER = RER × factor**, where **RER (Resting Energy Requirement) = 70 × (body weight in kg)^0.75** and the multiplier depends on age, neutering status, activity level, and body condition score.

The 0.75 exponent comes from **Kleiber's law (1932)**, the well-established biological observation that metabolic rate does not scale linearly with body weight: a dog that is twice as heavy burns roughly 1.68 times more calories, not 2 times. This metabolic scaling applies across virtually all mammals, from mice to elephants, and is the reason a 5 kg Chihuahua needs 234 kcal at rest while a 50 kg Mastiff needs only 1,304 kcal — about 5.6 times more for 10 times the weight.

This calculator applies the formula to **15 of the most popular breeds worldwide** with their typical activity factors, taking into account breed-specific traits such as Husky high energy versus Bulldog brachycephalic low tolerance for activity, Border Collie working drive versus toy breed sedentary lifestyle. The result tells you how many kcal per day your dog needs and converts that into grams of dry food based on the standard premium kibble caloric density of 380 kcal per 100 g. For non-standard foods (wet food at 90-110 kcal/100g, super-premium kibble at 410 kcal/100g, homemade at variable density) adjust the gram output proportionally.

Use this tool to: convert calorie targets into grams of your specific food brand by reading the kcal/100g on the bag label; plan a calorie deficit for weight loss (typically MER multiplied by 0.7-0.8 to drop 1-2 percent body weight per week); design homemade diets where you must hit a calorie target with chicken, rice, and vegetables; adjust portions for athletic activity (agility, canicross, hunting can multiply RER by 2-5); and answer the vet's question "how much are you feeding?" with a precise kcal-per-day figure rather than a vague "two cups."

**Important veterinary disclaimer:** The MER formula is a starting estimate, not a personalized prescription. Individual variation is significant — neutered dogs may need 20-25 percent fewer calories than the formula predicts, hypothyroid dogs need substantially less, very lean working dogs much more. Always validate the estimate by monitoring **body condition score (BCS, on a 1-9 scale)** at 4-6 weeks; if your dog gains weight while eating the formula amount, reduce by 10-15 percent; if losing, increase. Puppies and pregnant or lactating bitches have rapidly changing needs and should be monitored every 1-2 weeks. Consult your veterinarian for medical conditions, breed predispositions, or homemade diets.
keyTakeaway: **RER** (resting) = 70 × (weight^0.75). **MER adult neutered**: RER × 1.6. **Puppy**: RER × 2–3. **Active**: RER × 2–5. Premium kibble has ~380 kcal/100g.
useCases: Convert your dog's daily kcal target into grams of your specific food brand by reading the kcal/100g listed on the bag — example: 1,250 kcal needed divided by 380 kcal/100g equals 329 g of premium kibble per day.

Your 30 kg Labrador is overweight and you're calculating a 25 percent calorie deficit: full MER is 1,432 kcal/day, weight loss target equals 1,432 multiplied by 0.75, which equals 1,074 kcal/day to drop roughly 1.5 percent body weight per week.

Designing a homemade diet for a 15 kg adult dog requires a 950 kcal/day target, achievable with about 250 g cooked chicken (400 kcal), 200 g cooked rice (260 kcal), 150 g sweet potato (130 kcal), and balanced supplements — total about 950 kcal with proper protein-fat-carb ratios.

Your 4 kg Chihuahua puppy at 4 months needs about 200 kcal/day (RER 156 multiplied by puppy factor 2.0 equals 312 kcal, but smaller adjustments apply for toy breeds) — translates to roughly 50 g of premium puppy kibble divided into 3-4 small meals.

Your 25 kg adult Border Collie running 5 km of agility three times per week falls into the high activity category: MER equals 783 RER multiplied by 2.5, which equals 1,958 kcal/day — about 515 g of premium kibble, nearly double the sedentary equivalent.

Your 12-year-old senior Golden Retriever (32 kg) has reduced muscle mass and lower metabolism: senior factor 1.4 applied to RER 942 gives 1,319 kcal/day, down from 1,507 in adulthood — overfeeding seniors is a leading cause of senior obesity in 60+ percent of US dogs.

Your veterinarian asks for exact daily intake to evaluate a dietary issue: instead of saying 'about 2 cups of kibble,' you report '1,180 kcal divided into two meals of 590 kcal each, plus 50 kcal in training treats,' which is medically actionable.

Calculating cost-per-day of premium versus standard food: 25 kg Labrador needs about 1,250 kcal/day equals 329 g premium kibble at $4.50/kg or about $1.48/day, versus 379 g standard kibble at $2.80/kg or about $1.06/day — a 40 percent cost difference of $153/year.

explanation:
## MER Formula (Maintenance Energy Requirement)

```
RER = 70 × (weight_kg ^ 0.75)
MER = RER × factor
```

## Factors by Life Stage

| Life Stage | Factor |
|---|---|
| Puppy 2–4 months | 3.0 |
| Puppy 4–12 months | 2.0 |
| Adult intact active | 1.8 |
| Adult neutered | 1.6 |
| Adult sedentary (apartment, neutered) | 1.4 |
| Weight loss | 1.0 |
| Senior (>7 years) | 1.4 |
| Working / hunting / athletic | 2.0–5.0 |
| Pregnant (last third) | 3.0 |
| Lactating | 4–8 |

## Quick RER Reference Table

| Weight (kg) | RER (kcal) |
|---|---|
| 5 | 234 |
| 10 | 394 |
| 15 | 534 |
| 20 | 663 |
| 25 | 783 |
| 30 | 895 |
| 40 | 1,107 |
| 50 | 1,304 |

## Converting kcal to Grams of Dog Food

Check your food label (kcal/100g). Typical values:

- **Standard dry kibble**: 330 kcal/100g
- **Premium dry kibble**: 380 kcal/100g
- **Super premium dry kibble**: 410 kcal/100g
- **Wet/canned food**: 90–110 kcal/100g

faq.q: What is MER (Maintenance Energy Requirement) and how is it different from RER?
faq.a: **MER (Maintenance Energy Requirement)** is the total daily caloric intake your dog needs to maintain their current body weight given their normal activity, age, and reproductive status. **RER (Resting Energy Requirement)** is the baseline metabolic rate — the calories the dog would burn lying quietly in a thermoneutral environment. MER equals RER multiplied by a life-stage and activity factor: 1.4 for sedentary neutered adults, 1.6 for typical adults, 1.8 for intact adults, 2.0 for active working dogs, up to 5.0 for sled dogs in extreme work. Always start with RER, then apply the factor for your dog's specific situation. The 1.6 multiplier covers most family pets walked twice daily.

faq.q: Why does the formula use 0.75 as an exponent instead of 1.0?
faq.a: Because metabolic rate does not scale linearly with body weight — a phenomenon known as **Kleiber's law**, established by Max Kleiber in 1932. A dog that is twice as heavy does not burn twice the calories; it burns approximately 1.68 times more (2 to the 0.75 power). This biological scaling holds remarkably consistently across mammals from mice to elephants, because larger animals have proportionally lower surface-area-to-volume ratios and thus lose heat less rapidly. The 0.75 exponent ensures small dogs are not underfed and large dogs are not overfed, both of which would happen with a simple per-kilogram formula. WSAVA, FEDIAF, AAFCO, and most modern veterinary nutrition references use 0.75 as standard.

faq.q: How do I convert daily kcal to grams of my specific dog food brand?
faq.a: Read the **kcal per 100 grams** (sometimes labeled kcal ME/100g or metabolizable energy) on your food bag, then apply: grams equals daily kcal target divided by kcal per gram, multiplied by 100. Examples: 1,200 kcal divided by 380 kcal/100g equals 316 g of premium kibble; 1,200 kcal divided by 330 kcal/100g equals 364 g of standard kibble; 1,200 kcal divided by 410 kcal/100g equals 293 g of super-premium kibble. For wet food at 100 kcal/100g you would need 1,200 g (1.2 kg). If your bag does not list kcal density, contact the manufacturer — most have it on their website even if not printed on the bag. Quality brands always disclose it.

faq.q: How do I calculate calories for homemade dog meals?
faq.a: Add up the **kcal contribution of each ingredient**, using standard nutrition references. Common values per 100 g cooked: chicken breast 165 kcal, chicken thigh 209 kcal, lean beef 250 kcal, white rice 130 kcal, brown rice 112 kcal, sweet potato 86 kcal, carrots 41 kcal, broccoli 35 kcal, plain pumpkin 26 kcal, egg 155 kcal, salmon 208 kcal, plain yogurt 60 kcal. **Critical caveat**: a calorie-correct homemade diet is not necessarily nutritionally complete. Dogs require specific levels of calcium, phosphorus, vitamin D, taurine (in some breeds), zinc, and essential amino acids that home recipes commonly miss. Always consult a board-certified veterinary nutritionist (find one via ACVN.org) or use a verified balanced recipe from BalanceIT.com or PetDietDesigner.

faq.q: How much should I reduce my dog's calories for weight loss, and how fast should they lose?
faq.a: Feed **70 to 80 percent of full MER** to create a 20 to 30 percent calorie deficit, targeting a weight loss of **1 to 2 percent of body weight per week**. For a 30 kg Labrador this means losing about 300 to 600 g per week. Faster weight loss in dogs risks **hepatic lipidosis** (fatty liver), muscle wasting (sarcopenia), and nutrient deficiencies. The diet should be **higher in protein** (around 30 percent of metabolizable energy) than maintenance food to preserve lean mass, and fiber-rich to enhance satiety. Reweigh every 2 weeks. If weight stalls after 4-6 weeks, drop another 10 percent and increase walks. Always consult your vet first — sudden weight gain may signal hypothyroidism, Cushing's, or other medical conditions, not just overeating.

faq.q: Do dog treats count toward daily calorie intake?
faq.a: **Yes, absolutely** — and they are the single most underestimated source of canine obesity. A typical commercial treat has 5 to 20 kcal, but rawhide chews, bully sticks, and dental chews can reach 80-150 kcal each. Ten small training treats per day adds 50 to 200 kcal. The American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA) and WSAVA recommend that treats should not exceed **10 percent of daily total caloric intake**. For a 25 kg Labrador eating 1,250 kcal/day, this caps treats at 125 kcal — about 7 small Milk-Bone treats or 1 medium bully stick. Replace store treats with low-calorie alternatives like baby carrots (4 kcal each), green beans (3 kcal), or air-popped popcorn (30 kcal/cup) for active training without overfeeding.

faq.q: Is the 5 percent breed adjustment in this calculator scientifically justified?
faq.a: Yes. Veterinary nutrition research (Hand et al., Small Animal Clinical Nutrition, 5th edition; Laflamme 2012) has documented systematic differences in baseline energy needs across breeds. **High-energy breeds** (Border Collie, Siberian Husky, Jack Russell, working German Shepherds) burn 10-25 percent above formula baseline due to constant motor activity and lean body composition. **Brachycephalic breeds** (English Bulldog, French Bulldog, Pug) burn 10-15 percent below baseline due to exercise intolerance from upper-airway syndrome. **Giant breeds** (Mastiff, Great Dane, Saint Bernard) have slower metabolism per kg than the 0.75 formula predicts and need closer to 1.4 multipliers even when active. **Toy breeds** (Chihuahua, Yorkie) tend to have higher per-kg metabolism than the formula suggests. This calculator applies modest breed adjustments aligned with these references.

faq.q: What's the difference between calories needed for puppies versus adult dogs?
faq.a: Puppies require **2 to 3 times more calories per kg of body weight** than adults of the same breed during their rapid growth phase. The formula uses factor 3.0 for puppies 2-4 months (peak growth) and 2.0 for puppies 4-12 months (slowing growth). A 5 kg puppy at 3 months might need 700 kcal/day, while a 5 kg adult Chihuahua needs only 280 kcal. The mistake of feeding adult formula amounts to a growing puppy causes stunted growth, weak bones, and developmental orthopedic disease, especially in large and giant breeds where calcium-phosphorus imbalance during rapid growth predisposes to hip dysplasia and osteochondritis dissecans. **Large breed puppies** (over 25 kg adult weight) must use specifically formulated large-breed puppy food until 12-15 months of age.

faq.q: How do I determine if my dog is at a healthy weight or overweight?
faq.a: Use the **Body Condition Score (BCS)** on the standard 9-point WSAVA scale. A healthy adult dog scores **4 or 5 out of 9**: ribs easily palpable with minimal fat covering, visible waist when viewed from above, and a tucked abdomen when viewed from the side. Score 6 is overweight (ribs palpable with effort, waist barely visible), score 7 is obese (ribs not easily felt, fat deposits on back and tail base, no waist), and 8-9 is severely obese with major joint and metabolic risks. **About 56 percent of US dogs are overweight or obese** according to the Association for Pet Obesity Prevention 2024 survey, increasing cancer, diabetes, arthritis, and reducing lifespan by 1.5 to 2 years. Your vet can score precisely; an easy at-home check is whether you can feel ribs without pressing through fat layers.

faq.q: Should I feed my senior dog (over 7 years) differently than an adult?
faq.a: Yes, but the changes are less dramatic than commonly assumed. Senior dogs **lose 1-2 percent of muscle mass per year** without intervention, and their metabolic rate drops about 20-25 percent compared with adulthood, which is reflected in the senior factor of 1.4 instead of 1.6. However, recent research (Laflamme, Bartges, others) suggests senior dogs need **more protein, not less** — about 30-35 percent of metabolizable energy — to preserve lean mass and immune function, contradicting older 'low-protein-for-kidney-health' recommendations that applied only to dogs with diagnosed kidney disease. Monitor BCS more frequently in seniors (every 2-3 months) since dental issues, arthritis, and slow GI transit can cause unintentional weight loss. Joint supplements, omega-3 fatty acids, and slightly softer kibble texture often improve quality of life.

faq.q: Why does my neutered dog seem to gain weight on the same food amount?
faq.a: Neutering and spaying **reduce metabolic rate by 20 to 30 percent** due to hormonal changes that affect lean body mass and energy expenditure, while simultaneously **increasing appetite** by 25 to 50 percent through changes in leptin sensitivity. This dual effect means a dog fed the same amount post-neutering will gain weight rapidly — typically 0.5 to 1.5 kg within the first 6 months without intervention. The factor 1.6 (versus 1.8 for intact) compensates for this, but in practice many neutered dogs need to go further down to 1.4. **Action plan**: reduce food by 10-20 percent within 2 weeks of the surgery, monitor BCS monthly for 6 months, and resist the urge to compensate the bigger appetite with more food. Increased structured exercise (longer walks, fetch sessions) helps maintain lean mass.

faq.q: Can I trust the feeding guidelines printed on the dog food bag instead of calculating MER?
faq.a: **Use them as a rough starting point only.** Bag feeding charts are calibrated for a generic adult dog at moderate activity, often using the higher 1.8 multiplier suitable for intact active dogs. For about 60 percent of family pets — neutered, walked twice daily, mostly indoors — bag guidelines **overfeed by 15-30 percent**, contributing significantly to the obesity epidemic. Always calculate your dog's specific MER, then adjust the bag amount accordingly. Also note that bag guidelines use **cup volume**, which varies dramatically with kibble size and density: one cup of Royal Canin Mini equals 110 g but one cup of Hills Science Diet Large Breed equals 95 g. **Always weigh food on a kitchen scale** — even a 10 percent volume error compounds to 1-1.5 kg of weight gain per year.
